strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: improving the rate of short quaternary codes for insertion, deletion, and substitution errors. Using learned embeddings to prioritize codeword selection is a promising application of neural distance representations.

Algorithm 1 removes neighbors using exact Levenshtein distance, establishing minimum distance at least three independently of embedding accuracy. The resulting explicit codebooks therefore support exact single-error correction with an appropriate decoder.

Table 1 shows consistent improvements over random greedy selection across ten runs. At length 11, the best codebook contains 36,368 codewords, a 16.8% cardinality improvement and approximately one percentage point of additional code rate. The original-versus-revised loss ablation is useful.

The decoder reports zero failures in 100 million sampled corruptions per tested length with four retrieved neighbors. Synthetic data generation and a linked code repository support accessibility, and the paper acknowledges construction scalability limitations. The presented experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central density argument in Section 4.2 is unsupported. Batch normalization controls moments; it does not make embeddings jointly Gaussian. Furthermore, low fitted Gaussian density need not imply fewer Levenshtein neighbors in the remaining candidate set. The binary t-SNE visualization does not validate these relationships, and greedy selection only establishes a maximal codebook, not maximum cardinality.

The comparisons do not establish the claimed optimality or adequately isolate the contribution of learning. Stronger finite-length packing baselines, such as neighborhood-count-based greedy selection, lexicographic selection, or local search, are missing. Matching a proposed redundancy curve over a few short lengths supplies neither a tight bound nor an exact-optimum comparison. Although the lack of proof is acknowledged, the repeated optimality claims exceed the evidence.

The advertised combination of reliable correction and O(n) decoding is not established. The k=1 decoder fails on approximately 0.3–0.9% of trials, while the empirically reliable configuration uses exact verification that Section 5.5 analyzes as O(n²). Logarithmic k-d-tree query time also requires assumptions that are not justified for these 64-dimensional embeddings. Random trials cannot certify correction of every single-edit corruption; exhaustive checking is feasible at the reported codebook sizes.

The decoding benchmark uses an unnecessarily weak exact baseline. For a received word with at most one edit, one can enumerate O(n) possible original words of the required length and check codebook membership, avoiding a scan of every codeword. Thresholded edit-distance algorithms are also relevant. The general edit-distance hardness discussion does not justify excluding these alternatives, so the reported speedups do not establish an advantage attributable to the learned decoder.

The application evaluation assumes already isolated segments containing exactly one error. It does not evaluate recovery of segment boundaries after insertions or deletions, multiple errors within a segment, or outer-code overhead. Consequently, the proposed improvement in overall segmented-storage efficiency remains unquantified.

Reproducibility and computational cost are insufficiently documented in the manuscript. The training-pair distribution, handling of variable sequence lengths, complete network configuration, optimizer, training schedule, and hardware are unspecified. Runtime accounting does not clearly identify included preprocessing and embedding costs, and construction time and peak memory for enumerating all 4^n candidates are not reported. The repository link is helpful, but these omissions impede assessment of the claimed efficiency.
